chunks: Choosing scope bandwidth and sample rate. The question: What sample rate/bandwidth will I need to measure a signal?
Two scope specs decide whether a measurement can be trusted. Bandwidth says how fast a signal the scope's input can follow.
Sample rate says how many snapshots per second it takes.
You choose bandwidth from the fastest feature of the signal, then choose a sample rate high enough to draw that feature with several points.
Think of photographing a speeding car. Bandwidth is the camera's shutter: if it is too slow, the car smears into a blur no matter how many photos you take.
Sample rate is how many photos you take per second. Too few photos and you miss how the car moved. Fixing one does not fix the other.
if the scope's rise time equals the signal's, you read 41 % too slow; at 3 times faster it's 5 %; at 5 times it's 2 %.
This is where the "scope should be 3 to 5 times faster than the signal" rule comes from.
Bandwidth: the highest signal frequency the scope passes before readings start to shrink.
Sample rate: how many measurements per second the scope's converter (the part that turns voltage into numbers) takes.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to climb from 10% to 90% of its final value. Aliasing: false slower waveforms that appear when sampling is too slow.
Memory depth: how many samples the scope can store, which limits how long it can record at a given sample rate.
